etruscan-civilization.name: Etruscans
etruscan-civilization.summary: A civilization of ancient Italy formed by a federation of city-states, with the earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dating from about 900 BC and its territory reaching its greatest extent around 500 BC.

third-macedonian-war.name: Third Macedonian War
third-macedonian-war.summary: A 171–168 BCE war between Rome and King Perseus of Macedon, ending in Rome's victory at Pydna, the fall of the Antigonid dynasty, and the end of Macedon's independence.

baking-in-ancient-rome.name: Pistores
baking-in-ancient-rome.summary: Term for professional bakers in ancient Rome, first used after Greek bakers arrived in 171 BCE following the Third Macedonian War; bakers could grow wealthy but were often looked down upon.

principate.name: Principate
principate.summary: The early period of the Roman Empire, beginning with Augustus in 27 BC and lasting into the late third century, named for his title princeps, or leading citizen.

apicius.name: Apicius
apicius.summary: A collection of Roman cookery recipes, possibly compiled around the 5th century AD, traditionally but doubtfully attributed to a Roman gourmet of the same name.

oculus-architecture.name: Oculus
oculus-architecture.summary: A circular opening at the center of a dome or wall, originating in classical architecture and later used in Byzantine and Neoclassical buildings.

roman-concrete.name: Roman concrete
roman-concrete.summary: Hydraulic-setting cement material used in ancient Rome from about 150 BC, notable for its durability in structures like aqueducts and the Pantheon's dome.

nero.name: Nero
nero.summary: Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68, the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, remembered for orchestrating his mother's murder and for scandalous public performances as actor and musician.

domus-aurea.name: Domus Aurea
domus-aurea.summary: Vast landscaped palace complex built by Emperor Nero on Rome's Oppian Hill after the great fire of 64 AD destroyed much of the city.

grotesque.name: Grotesque style
grotesque.summary: An ornamental decorative art style based on Roman wall paintings found in Nero's ruined Domus Aurea, rediscovered and widely imitated from the Renaissance onward.

alexander-mosaic.name: Alexander Mosaic
alexander-mosaic.summary: A Roman floor mosaic from Pompeii's House of the Faun, dated to about 120–100 BC, depicting the battle between Alexander the Great and Darius III; now in Naples.

marcus-vipsanius-agrippa.name: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa
marcus-vipsanius-agrippa.summary: Roman general and statesman (c.63-12 BC), a close ally of Augustus known for his naval victory at Actium and for building the original Pantheon.

campus-martius.name: Campus Martius
campus-martius.summary: A large publicly owned area of ancient Rome, meaning 'Field of Mars'; it became the city's most populous district in the Middle Ages.

baths-of-agrippa.name: Baths of Agrippa
baths-of-agrippa.summary: The first great public bathhouse of ancient Rome, built by Marcus Agrippa; its remains were later absorbed into later buildings.

basilica-of-neptune.name: Basilica of Neptune
basilica-of-neptune.summary: An ancient Roman basilica built around 25 BCE by Marcus Agrippa in honour of Neptune, celebrating naval victories at Mylae, Naulochus and Actium.

hadrian.name: Hadrian
hadrian.summary: Roman emperor from 117 to 138, born in Hispania, who abandoned Trajan's territorial expansion in favor of stable borders and personally visited almost every province of the empire.

opus-tessellatum.name: Opus tessellatum
opus-tessellatum.summary: Standard Greek and Roman mosaic technique using tesserae larger than about 4 millimetres, laid directly at the final site and often paired with the finer opus vermiculatum for detailed panels.

opus-vermiculatum.name: Opus vermiculatum
opus-vermiculatum.summary: Fine mosaic technique using small tesserae to outline a subject with a smooth halo effect, considered one of the most demanding forms of mosaic work, often set against opus tessellatum.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

natural-history-pliny.name: Natural History
natural-history-pliny.summary: Encyclopedic Latin work by Pliny the Elder, published around AD 77, the largest surviving single work from the Roman Empire, covering topics from astronomy to art and precious stones.

caryatid.name: Caryatid
caryatid.summary: A sculpted female figure used as an architectural support in place of a column, named after the maidens of Karyai in ancient Greece who danced for the goddess Artemis.

hippodamus-of-miletus.name: Hippodamus of Miletus
hippodamus-of-miletus.summary: An ancient Greek architect and urban planner (c. 480–408 BC) regarded as the father of European urban planning, known for the grid-based 'Hippodamian plan' of city layout.

pax-romana.name: Pax Romana
pax-romana.summary: A roughly 200-year golden age of stability and expansion in ancient Rome, from Augustus's rise in 27 BCE to Marcus Aurelius's death in 180 CE.

senones.name: Senones
senones.summary: An ancient Gallic tribe from the Seine basin who joined revolts against Julius Caesar and, according to Roman accounts, sacked Rome around 390 BC after victory at the Battle of the Allia.

brennus.name: Brennus
brennus.summary: A Gaulish chieftain of the Senones who led an army of Cisalpine Gauls in their attack on Rome at the Battle of the Allia in 387 BC.

battle-of-the-allia.name: Battle of the Allia
battle-of-the-allia.summary: A battle fought around 387 BC in which Gallic Senones led by Brennus routed the Romans north of the city, leading to the sack of Rome and a day long remembered as ill-omened.

celtiberians.name: Celtiberians
celtiberians.summary: A group of Celts and Celticised peoples in central-northeastern Iberia in the final centuries BC, subjugated by Rome after a protracted struggle completed by 72 BC.

numantia.name: Numantia
numantia.summary: An ancient Celtiberian settlement in Spain that led resistance to Rome in the Celtiberian Wars until it was destroyed in 133 BC.

hispania.name: Hispania
hispania.summary: The Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula, divided into provinces under the Republic and Empire, and the source of the modern names Spain and Hispaniola.

battle-of-cape-ecnomus.name: Battle of Cape Ecnomus
battle-of-cape-ecnomus.summary: A 256 BC naval battle off Sicily in the First Punic War in which Rome defeated Carthage's fleet, possibly the largest sea battle in history by number of combatants.

battle-of-the-aegates.name: Battle of the Aegates
battle-of-the-aegates.summary: A naval battle fought on 10 March 241 BC near Sicily, in which Rome's fleet defeated Carthage's, ending the 23-year First Punic War and making Rome the leading power in the western Mediterranean.

social-war-91-87-bc.name: Social War
social-war-91-87-bc.summary: A war fought 91 to 88 BC between Rome and its rebelling Italian allies, largely ended by offering Roman citizenship to towns that had not revolted or laid down arms.

sulla.name: Sulla
sulla.summary: Roman general and statesman (138–78 BC) who became the first to march on Rome and win a civil war, then ruled as dictator and enacted constitutional reforms.

latin-war.name: Latin War
latin-war.summary: A 340–338 BC conflict between the Roman Republic and the Latin peoples of ancient Italy, ending with the dissolution of the Latin League and Rome absorbing its territory.

battle-of-trifanum.name: Battle of Trifanum
battle-of-trifanum.summary: A battle fought in 340 BC in which the Roman army under Manlius Imperiosus defeated the Latin League near the mouth of the Liri River, a victory so crushing the Latins soon surrendered.

samnites.name: Samnites
samnites.summary: An ancient Italic people of south-central Italy who fought three wars against Rome before being subjugated in 290 BCE and eventually assimilated.

battle-of-actium.name: Battle of Actium
battle-of-actium.summary: A naval battle fought on 2 September 31 BCE in which Octavian's fleet, aided by Marcus Agrippa, defeated the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, the climax of their long rivalry.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

mark-antony.name: Mark Antony
mark-antony.summary: Roman politician and general (83–30 BC) and ally of Julius Caesar who, after Caesar's assassination, formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and later allied with Cleopatra.

veii.name: Veii
veii.summary: An important ancient Etruscan city near Rome, the richest city of the Etruscan League, alternately at war and allied with Rome for over 300 years before falling to the Romans in 396 BC.

battle-of-the-cremera.name: Battle of the Cremera
battle-of-the-cremera.summary: A 477 BCE defeat of the Roman Republic by the Etruscan city of Veii, part of the long rivalry that ended with Veii's fall in 396 BCE.

etruria.name: Etruria
etruria.summary: A region of Central Italy between the Arno and Tiber rivers, home to the Etruscan civilization from around the 8th century BC until its absorption into the Roman Republic in the 4th century BC.

scipio-africanus.name: Scipio Africanus
scipio-africanus.summary: Roman general (236/235-c.183 BC) who defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, ending the Second Punic War and earning him the epithet 'Africanus'.

livy.name: Livy
livy.summary: A Roman historian (59 BC-AD 17) who wrote a monumental history of Rome, Ab Urbe Condita, from its legendary founding through Augustus's reign, and was a friend of Augustus.

hannibal.name: Hannibal
hannibal.summary: A Carthaginian general (247–183/181 BC) who led forces against Rome in the Second Punic War, famously crossing the Alps with war elephants to invade Italy.

servius-tullius.name: Servius Tullius
servius-tullius.summary: Legendary sixth king of Rome, reigning 578 to 535 BC, credited with victories over Veii and the Etruscans, expanding the city, and reforming Roman citizenship.

fasti-triumphales.name: Fasti Triumphales
fasti-triumphales.summary: A Roman calendar recording magistrates honored with triumphal processions for military victories, an important source for early Roman chronology discovered in fragments in 1546.

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.summary: Ancient Roman poet (70–19 BC) of the Augustan age who wrote the Eclogues, the Georgics and the epic Aeneid, becoming a hugely influential model for later Western literature.

aeneid.name: Aeneid
aeneid.summary: Latin epic poem by Virgil, written between 29 and 19 BC, telling of Aeneas's journey from Troy to Italy and his role as ancestor of the Romans.

aeneas.name: Aeneas
aeneas.summary: Trojan hero of Greco-Roman mythology, son of Anchises and Aphrodite, later cast in Virgil's Aeneid as an ancestor of Rome.

ovid.name: Ovid
ovid.summary: A Roman poet (43 BC – AD 17/18) ranked with Virgil and Horace, best known for the Metamorphoses, who was exiled by Augustus to the Black Sea for the rest of his life.

livius-andronicus.name: Livius Andronicus
livius-andronicus.summary: A Greco-Roman dramatist, actor and epic poet (c. 284-204 BC) regarded as the father of Roman drama, who translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin and wrote the first Latin plays.

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

saturnian-poetry.name: Saturnian meter
saturnian-poetry.summary: An old Latin poetic meter used before Greek verse forms took over; only around 132 complete lines survive, mostly from Livius Andronicus's translation of the Odyssey and Naevius's epic on the First Punic War.

gnaeus-naevius.name: Gnaeus Naevius
gnaeus-naevius.summary: Roman epic poet and dramatist (c. 270-201 BC) who fought in the Punic Wars, invented a new genre of tragedy on Roman themes, and was eventually exiled after satirizing a powerful family.

praetexta.name: Fabula praetexta
praetexta.summary: A genre of Latin tragedy introduced at Rome by Gnaeus Naevius in the 3rd century BC, dramatizing Roman historical figures instead of Greek myths; only one such play survives today.

augustine-of-hippo.name: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-of-hippo.summary: Christian theologian and Bishop of Hippo (354–430), one of history's most influential philosophers, known for works like Confessions and The City of God.

jerome.name: Jerome
jerome.summary: An early Christian priest, theologian and translator (c. 342–420) best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate); honored as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.

prudentius.name: Prudentius
prudentius.summary: Prudentius: A Roman Christian poet born in 348 in the Iberian Peninsula who died sometime after 405.

perpetua-and-felicity.name: Perpetua
perpetua-and-felicity.summary: A young noblewoman martyred with the enslaved Felicity at Carthage around 203 CE; her own prison narrative survives as part of the account of their deaths.

egeria-pilgrim.name: Egeria
egeria-pilgrim.summary: Hispano-Roman Christian woman believed to have written a detailed account, around 381–384, of a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, the earliest surviving text of its kind.

romulus.name: Romulus
romulus.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Rome, credited in tradition with establishing many of the city's earliest institutions, though how much is historical remains unclear.

romulus-and-remus.name: Remus
romulus-and-remus.summary: Twin brother of Romulus in Roman mythology, killed by Romulus before the legendary founding of Rome in 753 BC, part of a story symbolized by a she-wolf suckling the twins.

metamorphoses.name: Metamorphoses
metamorphoses.summary: A Latin narrative poem completed in 8 CE by the Roman poet Ovid, tracing world history through over 250 myths across 15 books; one of the most influential works in Western literature.

iphis.name: Iphis
iphis.summary: A figure in Greek and Roman mythology born female in Crete, raised as a boy, and later transformed into a man by the goddess Isis.

nisus-and-euryalus.name: Nisus and Euryalus
nisus-and-euryalus.summary: Two young warriors serving under Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, whose stealthy raid on the enemy ends in their tragic deaths together, and whose devoted bond has been read as romantic.

pietas.name: Pietas
pietas.summary: The ancient Roman virtue of duty, devotion and loyalty to gods, country and family, embodied by the hero Aeneas and a goddess of the same name.

reaper.name: Reaper
reaper.summary: A farm implement that cuts and gathers ripe crops, especially cereal grain; first documented as Gallic reapers used in Roman times, later mechanized in the 19th century.

herculaneum.name: Herculaneum
herculaneum.summary: Ancient Roman town near Naples buried by the 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius, whose volcanic material preserved even wooden objects and food.

vitruvius.name: Vitruvius
vitruvius.summary: Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BC whose De architectura is the only surviving ancient treatise on architecture, later inspiring Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man.

frontinus.name: Frontinus
frontinus.summary: Roman senator, general and engineer (c. 40-103 AD), best known as the author of technical treatises, especially one on Rome's aqueducts.

pons-aemilius.name: Pons Aemilius
pons-aemilius.summary: The oldest stone bridge in Rome, rebuilt in stone in the 2nd century BC to span the Tiber; only a single arch survives today, giving it the nickname 'Ponte Rotto,' the Broken Bridge.

archimedes.name: Archimedes
archimedes.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist and engineer from Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of all time for his work on geometry, levers and buoyancy.

ctesibius.name: Ctesibius
ctesibius.summary: A Greek inventor and mathematician in Alexandria around 285–222 BCE, called the 'father of pneumatics' for his work on compressed air and pumps, and inventor of an early pipe organ.

hero-of-alexandria.name: Hero of Alexandria
hero-of-alexandria.summary: Greek mathematician and engineer active in Roman-era Alexandria, seen as antiquity's greatest experimentalist; invented the steam-powered aeolipile and an early windwheel, and gave Heron's formula for triangle area.

euclid.name: Euclid
euclid.summary: An ancient Greek mathematician active around 300 BC, called the 'father of geometry' for his treatise Elements, which dominated the field of geometry until the 19th century.

latium.name: Latium
latium.summary: The region of central western Italy where Rome was founded; its name, meaning 'wide, flat', is the source of the word Latin.

princeps.name: Princeps
princeps.summary: A Latin title meaning 'first' or 'foremost', used for the leading member of the Roman Senate and later adopted by Augustus as an unofficial title for the Roman emperor.

imperium.name: Imperium
imperium.summary: Form of authority in ancient Rome held by magistrates such as consuls and praetors to control a military unit, province, or governmental entity.

romulus-augustulus.name: Romulus Augustulus
romulus-augustulus.summary: Last Western Roman emperor, a child figurehead who ruled from 475 to 476 CE before being deposed by the general Odoacer, an event marking the end of the Western Roman Empire.

odoacer.name: Odoacer
odoacer.summary: A barbarian soldier who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476 CE and ruled Italy until 493, an event traditionally marking the end of the Western Roman Empire.

ostrogoths.name: Ostrogoths
ostrogoths.summary: A Germanic people who founded a kingdom in Italy in 493 under Theodoric the Great; their state collapsed by 554 after a long war with the Byzantine Empire.

first-punic-war.name: First Punic War
first-punic-war.summary: First of three wars between Rome and Carthage, fought 264–241 BC mainly over Sicily, ending in Roman victory and Rome's first overseas provinces.

julius-caesar.name: Julius Caesar
julius-caesar.summary: Roman general and statesman, 100 to 44 BC, who became dictator of the Republic, expanded Roman territory through the Gallic Wars, and was assassinated in 44 BC.

battle-of-philippi.name: Battle of Philippi
battle-of-philippi.summary: The final 42 BC battle of the Liberators' civil war, fought in two engagements at Philippi in Macedonia, in which Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Julius Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius, who both died by suicide.

diocletian.name: Diocletian
diocletian.summary: Roman emperor from 284 to 305 who ended the Crisis of the Third Century and began splitting the empire by creating the Tetrarchy, sharing rule with three co-emperors.

mediolanum.name: Mediolanum
mediolanum.summary: The ancient city where Milan now stands, founded by the Insubres around 590 BCE, conquered by Rome in 222 BCE and later made an imperial capital under Maximian.

tiberius.name: Tiberius
tiberius.summary: Second Roman emperor, ruling from AD 14 to 37 as Augustus's stepson and successor, and earlier one of Rome's most successful generals.

praetorian-prefect.name: Praetorian prefect
praetorian-prefect.summary: A high Roman office established by Augustus in 2 BC, originally commander of the Praetorian Guard, which grew into the emperor's chief aide and later a top territorial administrator.

sejanus.name: Sejanus
sejanus.summary: A Roman soldier and confidant of Emperor Tiberius who commanded the Praetorian Guard from AD 14 until his execution for treason in AD 31, controlling Rome's administration in his later years.

naevius-sutorius-macro.name: Naevius Sutorius Macro
naevius-sutorius-macro.summary: Prefect of the Roman Praetorian Guard from 31 to 38 AD under emperors Tiberius and Caligula, who killed himself after falling from favor.

cato-the-elder.name: Cato the Elder
cato-the-elder.summary: Roman senator, soldier and historian (234-149 BC) known for conservatism; elected consul in 195 BC and censor in 184 BC, and the first to write Roman history in Latin.

lex-oppia.name: Lex Oppia
lex-oppia.summary: A Roman law of 215 BC, passed after the disaster at Cannae, restricting women's gold, colourful clothing and use of carriages; repealed in 195-193 BC despite Cato the Elder's opposition.

theodoric-the-great.name: Theodoric the Great
theodoric-the-great.summary: King of the Ostrogoths (471–526) who ruled Italy and controlled a realm stretching from the Atlantic to the Adriatic, exercising imperial powers recognized by Constantinople.

boethius.name: Boethius
boethius.summary: Roman senator, consul and philosopher (c. 480–524 CE) who translated Greek classics into Latin, becoming a central bridge between Classical and Christian scholarship.

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras
pythagoras.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (c. 570–495 BC) from Samos, founder of Pythagoreanism, later credited with the Pythagorean theorem and the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

parmenides.name: Parmenides
parmenides.summary: A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Elea, active around 500 BC, whose surviving poem argues that reality is unchanging, timeless, and one.

zeno-of-elea.name: Zeno of Elea
zeno-of-elea.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 490–c. 430 BC) from Elea who devised famous paradoxes denying plurality and motion in defense of his teacher Parmenides' philosophy of monism.

empedocles.name: Empedocles
empedocles.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Sicily (c. 494–434 BC) best known for the theory of the four classical elements, mixed and separated by forces he called Love and Strife.

gorgias.name: Gorgias
gorgias.summary: Ancient Greek sophist and rhetorician (c. 483–375 BC) from Sicily who helped bring rhetoric and the Attic dialect to mainland Greece.

carneades.name: Carneades
carneades.summary: Greek philosopher (214/3–129/8 BC) and leading head of the Skeptical Academy, known for challenging Stoic and Epicurean doctrines and for a theory of plausibility based on reasonable evidence.

diogenes-of-babylon.name: Diogenes of Babylon
diogenes-of-babylon.summary: Stoic philosopher (c. 230–c. 150/140 BC) who led the Stoic school in Athens and was sent as one of three philosophers on an embassy to Rome in 155 BC.

critolaus.name: Critolaus
critolaus.summary: Greek Peripatetic philosopher (c. 200–118 BC) from Phaselis, one of three philosophers sent to Rome in 155 BC, who wrote on rhetoric and ethics and considered pleasure an evil.

mos-maiorum.name: Mos maiorum
mos-maiorum.summary: The unwritten code of ancestral custom that shaped ancient Roman social norms, central to Roman traditionalism alongside written law.

classical-element.name: Four classical elements
classical-element.summary: Earth, water, fire and air, proposed in ancient Greece to explain all matter; devised by Empedocles and later systematized by Aristotle.

insula-building.name: Insula
insula-building.summary: A type of Roman apartment building that housed most of ancient Rome's urban population, while the wealthiest elite lived in single-family homes called a domus.

vestal-virgin.name: Vestal Virgins
vestal-virgin.summary: Priestesses of Vesta, Rome's goddess of the hearth, chosen before puberty to tend the sacred flame and vow chastity for at least thirty years, with severe penalties for failure.

battle-of-cannae.name: Cannae
battle-of-cannae.summary: A 216 BC battle of the Second Punic War in southern Italy where Hannibal's Carthaginian army encircled and annihilated a much larger Roman force, one of the deadliest single days of fighting in history.

pontifex-maximus.name: Pontifex Maximus
pontifex-maximus.summary: The chief high priest of ancient Rome's College of Pontiffs; originally a religious post, it grew increasingly political and was absorbed into the role of emperor beginning with Augustus.

piazza-venezia.name: Piazza Venezia
piazza-venezia.summary: A central Rome square where major roads meet, named after the Palazzo Venezia built for Cardinal Pietro Barbo, who later became Pope Paul II.

hortensia-orator.name: Hortensia
hortensia-orator.summary: Roman orator active around 42 BC, daughter of consul Quintus Hortensius, known for a speech before the Second Triumvirate that led to a partial repeal of a tax on wealthy Roman women.

roman-triumph.name: Roman triumph
roman-triumph.summary: A ceremonial procession in ancient Rome celebrating a victorious general, who paraded through the city with his army and spoils before sacrificing to Jupiter.

tacitus.name: Tacitus
tacitus.summary: A Roman historian and politician (c. 56–120 AD) whose works Annals and Histories chronicled the empire, regarded as one of Rome's greatest historians.

cybele.name: Cybele
cybele.summary: Anatolian mother goddess dating back to earliest Neolithic Çatalhöyük, adopted by the Greeks and later worshipped in Rome as 'Magna Mater', linked to mountains, fertility and wild animals.

phrygia.name: Phrygia
phrygia.summary: A civilization and kingdom in west-central Anatolia centered on the Sangarios River, which reached its peak under King Midas in the late 8th century BC before falling to Cimmerian raiders and later Lydian, Persian and Hellenistic rule.

theodosius-ii.name: Theodosius II
theodosius-ii.summary: Roman emperor from 402 to 450 who issued the Theodosian law code, built Constantinople's Theodosian walls, and founded the world's oldest university there in 425.
